item.title: The Houthis On the March
item.description: A Saudi offensive against the Houthis would doom the United States’ war effort in the Middle East.
item.dc:creator: Predictive History
item.content:encoded:
In December 2024, Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) in their pick-up trucks launched a probing attack against the Assad government in Syria. To everyone’s surprise, a 170,000-strong army that had weathered 14 years of civil war suddenly withered into the desert wind. Bashar al-Assad, a London-trained ophthalmologist who inherited his father’s brutal dictatorship, fled to Moscow, and the HTS leader Ahmed Al-Sharaa, an internationally-sanctioned terrorist, picked up the crown.

The Assad government’s sudden collapse was a devastating blow to the Axis of Resistance. Iran could no longer use the Syrian land bridge to supply Hezbollah, and Israel now had the Syrian air bridge to strike Tehran. Eighteen months later, Israel launched Operation Rising Lion, and initiated the 12-day War.

And the rest is history. If Syria had not fallen, there would still be a precarious peace in the Middle East today.

With Ansar Allah’s recent push towards the Yemeni coast, we may experience a similar inflection point.

Ansar Allah (more commonly referred to as the Houthis) have been at war since 2014. Yemen is an unwieldy Hodge-podge of tribes, and the insurgent Houthis fought against the government of Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, who called upon his patron Saudi Arabia to intervene. The Houthis are Shia Muslims, and Iran’s Middle East envoy Qassem Soleimani (who would later be assassinated in a drone strike ordered by Trump on January 3rd, 2020) cultivated them as a counter to Saudi Arabia, which was Iran’s main regional rival.

Hoping to emulate the United States’ successful 1991 “Desert Storm” campaign to dislodge the Iraqis from Kuwait, the Saudis initially committed 150,000 troops and 100 warplanes against the Houthis in operation “Decisive Storm.”

The Saudis also organized a broad coalition. The United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Sudan, Jordan, Morocco, Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain all provided direct military support. The United States, the United Kingdom, and France provided arms, intelligence, and targeting to the coalition.

After spending tens of billions of dollars without effect, Saudi Arabia was forced to sign an UN-brokered truce in 2022. The fanatical Houthis could not be starved into submission, and while the Saudi coalition could never penetrate into the Houthi mountains the Houthis could easily burn down the Saudi energy infrastructure with their Iran-supplied drones and ballistic missiles. The Saudis learned the hard way that the Houthis could never be defeated as long as Iran was still standing. (This was a reason why Saudi Arabia urged Trump to start his war against Iran.)

The United States would also learn the tenacity of the Houthis. In response to the Gaza genocide, the Houthis disrupted Red Sea shipping. President Joe Biden organized a twenty-nation campaign called Operation Prosperity Guardian on December 18, 2023 to counter the Houthi disruption. The campaign was a failure from the start, and on May 6, 2025 President Donald Trump ordered a unilateral withdrawal.

The Houthis did not join the war when the United States and Israel first bombarded Iran on February 28 of this year. Saudi Arabia and the Houthis had a precarious peace, and on July 13th Saudi Arabia launched an air-strike on Houthi-held Sanaa International Airport, supposedly to prevent an Iranian plane from landing. In retaliation, the Houthis resumed threatening Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. On August 7th, Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defense pact called the Mecca Accords with Turkey and Pakistan.

This defense pact is already being tested. This week, in a probing attack, the Houthis surprised everyone, probably including themselves, by spreading far and wide, as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces withered into the desert wind. This Thursday, the Houthis captured Mokha, a vital Red Sea port. Then they captured Perim, a strategic island that cements the Houthi control over the strategic Bab El-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis now control Yemen’s Red Sea coastline, and together with Iran they dictate the flow of 30 percent of the world’s energy.

item.title: Spy Versus Spy
item.description: John Ratcliffe visits Russia, as Putin prepares for war against NATO.
item.dc:creator: Predictive History
item.content:encoded:
In the 1975 movie “Dog Day Afternoon,” Sonny Wortzik (played by Al Pacino) and Salvatore “Sal” Naturile (played by John Cazale) hold up a bank, take hostages, and demand to flee in a private plane. FBI Special Agent Sheldon (played by James Broderick) arrives at the scene, and asks to check up on the well-being of the hostages. He is there not to see the hostages, but to size up the two bank robbers.

By studying the anxiety in their faces, Sheldon determines that Sonny cannot kill, but Sal will. “We’ll take care of Sal,” Sheldon whispers to Sonny, who replies without conviction that he’ll never betray his friend.

The FBI agrees to all terms, and sends a car and driver. Sonny calls out the driver as a plant, causing immediate dismay and consternation among the FBI agents. Sonny is just too smart for them. He singles out the biggest nerd among the FBI agents, and designates him as their driver, unwittingly co-operating in his own doom. During the bumpy ride, the FBI “nerd” pulls out a gun from a hidden compartment, and shoots Sal in the head.

A long time ago, I used to play a lot of Texas Hold’em poker, and I would observe opponents staring down each other to figure out each other’s hole cards. It took some time before I realized that they just weren’t interested in the hole cards. They were sizing each other out, and planning for the future. The best players would make an obvious bluff or let one slide to trick their opponent into making a riskier, more costly play in the future. All of this was subconscious and intuitive, invisible to even themselves.

This Tuesday, John Ratcliffe, Trump’s CIA Director, secretly visited Moscow for a few hours to meet with his Russian counterparts, and he may or may not have met with Putin. The Wall Street Journal reported that he was there to warn the Russians against further aggression, and Trump himself downplayed the visit as “semi-routine.”

The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was in November 2021 when William Burns went uninvited to warn against an invasion of Ukraine. Burns threatened dire retaliation, and Putin (having sized up Biden accurately) went ahead with the invasion three months later. So Ratcliffe’s visit is significant, and one mystery is whether he met with Putin.

There are some analysts who see Ratcliffe as a war hawk, and his intelligence assessment that Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon was a major reason why Trump went to war against Iran. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard (who argued against this assessment) clashed repeatedly with Ratcliffe.

With her resignation the war hawks within the Trump administration seem ascendant, but Ratcliffe got to where he is because he has demonstrated intense personal loyalty to Trump. As a Congressman, he attacked Mueller’s investigation into Trump’s Russia ties, and was Trump’s main champion during the impeaching hearings in Congress. As director of national intelligence in Trump’s first term and as director of the CIA in his second, Ratcliffe released classified documents that favored Trump politically. Ratcliffe won out in his clash with Gabbard because Trump trusted him in a way that he could not trust her.

This suggests that Ratcliffe went to Russia as Trump’s emissary to deliver a message that could only be delivered in person. If he had gone to Russia to set red lines (as most reporting suggests) then this could have done through diplomatic channels – or he could have just given a press conference.

I understand that both the Russians and the Americans denied Ratcliffe met with Putin – but game theory suggests they had to meet. What then was the message that Trump wanted delivered to Putin personally?

item.title: The Trump Whisperers
item.description: Who is Natalie Harp, and what does she want? Probably the same thing that Benjamin Netanyahu and Sean Hannity want.
item.dc:creator: Predictive History
item.content:encoded:
A young woman becomes obsessed with the President of the United States, and connives her way into the White House. Their relationship becomes a national scandal, with peace in the Middle East hanging in the balance.

I am referring to Monica Lewinsky and Bill Clinton, but I could have also been referring to Natalie Harp and Donald Trump.

In July 1995, a major Democratic donor Walter Kaye got a young Lewis & Clark graduate an internship at the White House, the most prestigious position a young person with political aspirations could obtain (Lewinsky had no political ambitions). Starting in November 1995, for eighteen months, Lewinsky had an affair with Bill Clinton (who was attracted to busty brunettes as much as Trump was attracted to tall blondes).

After Lewinsky was transferred from the White House to the Pentagon, she confided about the affair to a colleague, Linda Tripp. Tripp was persuaded by a literary agent (and Republican operative) named Lucianne Goldberg to tape the conversations, and these tapes led to the Starr Report, which then led to the impeachment of Bill Clinton and the derailment of his second term agenda (the major foreign policy objective being the Oslo Peace Accords, which sought to create a two-state solution to end the Israel-Palestine conflict).

This past week, the American public learned about 35-year old Natalie Harp’s obsession with 80-year old Donald Trump. In October 2023, while in New York City, Harp jumped into the trunk of an SUV of Trump’s motorcade rather than be away from him. In 2024, Trump staffers denied a room to Harp at Trump’s Bedminster golf club in New Jersey, and so she slept in the locker room that summer. There is a picture from May 2023 of Harp, like a loyal dog, happily sprinting after Trump as he sped ahead in his golf cart.

item.title: China's Art of the Compromise
item.description: In a world at war, China seeks peace, and is thus doomed.
item.dc:creator: Predictive History
item.content:encoded:
There is a remarkable new film in China that has become a blockbuster. “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” is a tragi-comedy that follows the travails of a Chinese chef sent to the Middle East to pay off family debts. The country he finds himself in – which is Iraq, although it is not named – is invaded by the Americans, and the chef finds himself trying to navigate imperial thuggery and religious extremism.

His restaurant is destroyed in the invasion, and when his boss turns insurgent the Americans sweep up the chef in a raid. He cooks in prison for his fellow prisoners, and the Americans exonerate him. But then insurgents pull a prison break, and he finds himself cooking for them. He witnesses children being indoctrinated to become suicide bombers, and after befriending them he concocts a crazy scheme to free them. The protagonist wants no part in a war he can never understand, but he refuses to abandon innocent children.

It took two years for the Chinese censors to approve the film for release, and the timing has proven to be perfect. Covid has collapsed the Chinese economy, and ordinary Chinese are struggling to make ends meet while trying to make sense of the chaos in the Middle East, which threatens to destroy the global economy. There is a sense of dread and hopelessness in China, and Chinese all ask, “Why can’t we just get along, and enjoy a good meal together?”

This despair was compounded with the news this week of the death of Premier Zhu Rongji at age 97. In 1998, after the death of supreme leader Deng Xiaoping, he partnered with President Jiang Zemin to bring China into the World Trade Organization. In moving from Shanghai to Beijing, Zhu correctly understood that China needed a Singapore-like meritocratic bureaucracy if it were to transition successfully, and he promised a hundred coffins, 99 for the most corrupt officials and one for himself. Rumors were that the entrenched elite (who controlled the military as well as the state-owned enterprises) sent him their response when they assassinated dozens of his closest allies and relatives. Faced with such thuggery and terror, Zhu did what all Chinese leaders tend to do, and he compromised. The largest state-owned enterprises continued to be parasites on the Chinese state, and the rest were allowed to be asset-stripped by local elites.

item.title: Twilight of the Meritocracy
item.description: Abdul Al-Sayed is insurgent, and many hope this is the Democrats' Tea Party moment. Voters, who hate the meritocracy more than war, may differ.
item.dc:creator: Predictive History
item.content:encoded:
This Tuesday, Abdul Al-Sayed, a forty-one year old doctor and Rhodes Scholar, energized the anti-war left to defeat Haley Stevens, who had received over $30 million dollar from AIPAC and $60 million overall. The two competed to be the Democratic nominee to replace Gary Peters (D) as a Senator from Michigan, always a crucial swing state. It was a close race, with Abdul Al-Sayed eking out a one-percentage victory in an election with 1.5 million ballots counted. Gretchen Whitmer and Chuck Schumer had supported Stevens in the primary, and now have endorsed Al-Sayed for the general election.

Israel and Zionism are now toxic issues in the United States. Sixty-percent of Americans view Israel unfavorably, and Israel is quickly losing support among evangelical Christians and young Jews. In a sign of the times, Jon Stewart told John Fetterman, who seems to care only about one issue, that anti-Zionism and anti-Semitism should not be conflated, and that it is proper and right for everyone to call out Israel’s genocide.

AIPAC is quick to dispel the notion that Al-Sayed’s victory is a harbinger, and that they are on the wane. AIPAC is Israel First, and they point out thirty AIPAC-candidates have advanced to the November mid-terms. They highlight the fact that former Missouri congresswoman Cori Bush, a fierce and effective critic of Israel, was defeated in her Democratic primary.

On the right, Tucker Carlson, Marjorie Taylor-Greene, Thomas Massie, and Joe Kent have announced a new America First movement in response to Trump’s betrayal. Cenk Uygur is excited about their platform, and believes that anti-Zionism could be a unifying issue for the left and right, ending decades of political polarization.

item.title: Welcome to the Point of No Return
item.description: The MOU between the United States and Iran is dead, and the war is spreading across the region. Trump jokes, as the world burns.
item.dc:creator: Predictive History
item.content:encoded:
Analysts expect a heavy bombardment of Iran this weekend, as well as swift Iranian retaliation. We have reached the point of no return, and there are three clear signs this week that the war can only escalate.

The most important is that the Houthis have jumped into the war, closing the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Saudi shipping, which may cut another 7 percent of oil from the global supply. In retaliation to Saudi attacks the Houthis have targeted an Aramco facility in Jazan, Saudi Arabia, demonstrating how vulnerable the country’s energy infrastructure is to Houthi drones and missiles.

This conflict would not have been started unless the Saudis had made the conscious decision to end the Houthi threat once and for all, and the Houthis had assurances from the Iranians. There is no way to close the Pandora’s Box that is the Houthis once it is opened. They are a poor, isolated, and fanatical people who are shielded inside their high mountains. In their ten-year struggle with the Houthis, the Saudis wasted anywhere from $100 billion to $260 billion. During Operation Prosperity Guardian, the world’s most powerful navy failed to prevent the Houthis from harassing Red Sea shipping.

The only way to dislodge the Houthis from their mountain fortress would be a ground invasion — possibly a multinational mercenary force financed by the Saudis. Trump has signed a deal to sell nuclear power plants to Saudi Arabia, and this can be construed as a Saudi bribe to incentivize the United States to deal with the Houthis. Because of Israeli pressure, Trump has made a condition for any nuclear deal that Saudi Arabia join the Abraham Accords, a move that would be unpopular at home. Eventually the Saudis will be forced to make a deal in order to push all-in against the Houthis, who will always remain an existentialist threat.

item.title: The Perfect Storm
item.description: The Bronze Age collapse began with wars, earthquakes, and droughts. So will ours.
item.dc:creator: Predictive History
item.content:encoded:
It is possible to ignore war, but not the weather.

El Nino is an intense warming of the world’s oceans, which has led to extreme weather around the world. Heatwaves in Europe and India have killed thousands. Violent storms and flooding have spread across the world. This week alone, flooding in southern China has killed 39, and hurricanes in central China have killed 11. In Beijing, where I live, the heat has been as intense as the rain.

In the past two months, there have been thirteen serious earthquakes, including two that struck Venezuela on the same day. So far, nearly four thousand have been confirmed dead, with 16,740 still missing.

These extreme geophysical events may unleash a chain reaction that culminates with empty shelves in the most privileged parts of the world and starving children in the least.

It does not help that there seems to be no political solution to either the war in Iran or in Ukraine. In fact, it seems both wars are about to escalate. NATO leaders met in Ankara this week, and Trump agreed to permit Ukraine to manufacture the Patriot air defense system.
